During the first trimester the baby's main organs form. The heart starts beating around week 6, and the neural tube (which becomes the brain and spinal cord) closes in these early weeks.
In the second trimester you usually start to feel the baby's first movements. Bones harden, senses like hearing develop and growth speeds up noticeably.
In the third trimester the baby gains weight quickly and the lungs finish maturing to breathe air outside the womb. The baby usually settles head-down ready for birth.

Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last period (LMP), not from the day of conception. It's the standard medical convention because most women remember that date more precisely than the exact day of ovulation.

That's why in "week 4" of pregnancy the baby has actually only been growing for about 2 weeks since conception: the first 2 weeks of the count are before ovulation happened.

With twins, the date is calculated at 37 weeks (259 days) from your last period, instead of the 40 weeks of a single pregnancy — a full-term multiple pregnancy is shorter because there's less room in the womb.

It's only an estimated date: many twin births happen even earlier, between weeks 36 and 37.

It's calculated with Naegele's rule: your last period + 280 days (40 weeks). It's only an estimated date, not an exact one — it's calculated this way because a full-term pregnancy lasts 40 weeks on average from the LMP.

In practice, very few babies are born exactly on that day: most arrive within a couple of weeks before or after.

The belly grows more noticeably; some back pain may appear.

You're halfway through the pregnancy — this is usually when the anatomy scan happens.
If you can, go with her to that appointment — seeing the baby together is usually a very special moment.
The baby's movements become clearer and more frequent.

Offer her moisturizer and help her put her feet up when she rests on the sofa.
Mild, painless contractions (Braxton Hicks) may start to be felt now and then.
Reassure her if they worry her — they're normal, but encourage her to mention them at her next appointment if she has questions.
She may get heartburn or indigestion more often as the uterus grows.
Suggest smaller, more frequent meals together instead of big plates.
Leg cramps, especially at night, are quite common at this stage.
A gentle calf stretch before bed, done together with her, can help.
She may find it hard to get comfortable to sleep.
Get her extra pillows to support her back or to put between her knees when sleeping on her side.
The second trimester ends — tiredness may gradually return.
It's a good time to pick up the conversation about the birth plan together.
The third trimester begins; doctor's appointments usually become more frequent.
Help her organize the upcoming appointments and, if you can, go with her to some.
Shortness of breath when moving is normal — the uterus pushes up against the lungs.
Don't rush her when walking; let her set her own pace.
Sleep may be harder because of shortness of breath, heartburn or simply the size of the bump.
Be understanding if she sleeps badly — avoid planning very demanding activities for the next day.
She may feel clumsier or heavier when moving, which is totally expected at this point.
Offer help with tasks that involve bending down or lifting, without her having to ask.
Swelling in the feet and ankles may increase, especially at the end of the day.
Encourage her to put her feet up for a while each afternoon, and offer a massage if she'd like.
The baby moves less due to lack of space, but the movements are stronger.
This is a good time to finish getting the nursery or the hospital bag ready together.
She may feel more anxious or nervous, which is normal as the due date approaches.
Listen if she wants to talk about her fears about labor, without downplaying them or trying to "fix" them.
She may feel more pressure in her pelvis as the baby settles into position for birth.
Go over the route to the hospital and what to bring together — having it ready gives you both peace of mind.
Appointments are usually weekly from now on; she may feel impatient for the moment to arrive.
Keep your phone close and the important things at hand — labor may come early.
The pregnancy is now considered "early term" — the baby could be born at any moment.
Confirm the plan together: who to call, how to get to the hospital, who looks after other children if there are any.
She may feel the "nesting instinct": the urge to clean, tidy up and get everything ready.
Help her with those tasks instead of telling her to rest — for many, doing them is calming.
The wait may feel long; practice contractions may become more frequent.
Be patient with the uncertainty of "when will it be" — she'd like to know too.
It's the due date, although many babies are born a few days before or after.
Stay calm and have everything ready — your calmness helps her feel calmer too.

One morning, Michi found a letter under the door. It had a drawing of the moon and said: "Whoever lovingly looks after their favourite person may come and visit me." Michi looked at you… and knew that person was you.
Michi packed his backpack: a ball of yarn, three fish biscuits and a photo of you. "So I don't feel alone," he whispered. And he went out into the garden with his tail held high.
In the garden, the flowers turned to greet him. A daisy told him: "To reach the moon, follow the river and never give up." Michi thanked her with a purr.
A butterfly was crying because she couldn't find her family. Michi walked with her to the biggest rose bush, where they were waiting. "Kindness always comes back," the butterfly told him.
The wooden bridge creaked and Michi's little paws were shaking. He took a deep breath, just like you taught him, and crossed it step by step. The fish clapped their fins.
Suddenly it started to rain. Michi sheltered under a huge leaf and thought of you. "Storms pass too," he told himself. And soon a rainbow appeared.
On the hill there were balloons of every colour. Michi jumped and jumped until he caught a pink one. Holding it, he floated above the clouds for a little while.
There he met Luna, a little white cat who collected stars. "Are you going to the moon palace? I'll show you the way!" From that day on, they travelled together.
The castle was made of cotton clouds. King Cloud offered them hot chocolate and told them a secret: "The moon shines brighter when someone is waiting for it."
After so much walking, Michi and Luna slept on a bed of clouds. Michi dreamed of you and smiled in his sleep. Resting is part of the journey too.
When they woke up, a cloud set them down on a beach of pink sand. The waves sounded like a giant purr. Michi dipped his paws in the water and laughed.
Luna found a seashell that sang old songs. One of them went: "Every day you look after yourself is a step towards the moon." Michi learned it by heart.
The trees were lollipops and the river was a strawberry milkshake. Michi tried a little of everything… and got a tummy ache! He learned that sweet things are best in small doses.
In the middle of the forest there was a maze. Michi got lost, but he looked at your photo, calmed down and found the way out.
They reached a lake that reflected a thousand stars. A little paper boat was waiting for them. They rowed in silence, listening to the water.
A shooting star fell near the boat. Michi caught it carefully and made a wish: "May my favourite person always be happy."
Luna had to go back to her family. They hugged tightly. "True friends always find each other," she said. Michi gave her his star.
At the end of the lake, a staircase of light appeared, climbing up to the sky. It had a hundred steps. Michi climbed them one by one, unhurried, the way important things are done.
The Moon welcomed him with a huge smile. "You made it because you never stopped looking after your person," she said. And she gave him a little of her glow.
Michi got home just in time to see you. He gave you the moon's glow with a purr. Ever since, whenever you look after yourself, that glow is inside you. The end 🌙
